notes.front: What is an authorization mode in Kubernetes?
notes.back: A way the API server decides whether an authenticated request is allowed: AlwaysAllow, AlwaysDeny, ABAC, RBAC, Node or Webhook.
notes.explanation: Several modes can be chained; each is consulted in the order the cluster administrator configures.
notes.example: Like several checkpoints a request passes through, each able to wave it through, turn it away, or shrug.

notes.front: What are the three possible authorization verdicts?
notes.back: Allow, deny, or no opinion; the first module to allow or deny wins, and if all give no opinion the request is denied.
notes.explanation: Access is denied by default: staying silent is not the same as approving.
notes.example: Like a panel of judges: the moment one clearly votes yes or no, the vote is decided.

notes.front: What does the AlwaysAllow authorization mode do?
notes.back: It allows every request, bypassing authorization entirely; the docs warn never to use it on a publicly reachable API server.
notes.explanation: It is meant only for testing, since it removes the one check standing between an authenticated request and full access.
notes.example: Like a door with no lock at all, left open for convenience during setup.

notes.front: What is Node authorization?
notes.back: A special-purpose authorization mode that grants a kubelet permissions based on the Pods scheduled to run on its node.
notes.explanation: It limits a kubelet's permissions to what the Pods on its own node need.
notes.example: Like giving a site foreman keys only to the buildings on their own site.

notes.front: What is the ABAC authorization mode?
notes.back: Attribute-based access control: access rights come from policies that combine attributes of the user, resource and environment.
notes.explanation: Its attributes still describe the same requests RBAC reasons about.
notes.example: Like a rule that checks several conditions at once: who you are, what you're touching, and when.

notes.front: What is Webhook authorization?
notes.back: A synchronous HTTP callout that blocks the request until a remote service replies with a decision.
notes.explanation: It lets an organisation plug its own custom policy engine into the authorization chain.
notes.example: Like pausing at a gate while a call is made to confirm you're allowed through.

notes.front: What are request verbs?
notes.back: The action names Kubernetes maps HTTP methods to for authorization: get, list, watch, create, update, patch, delete, deletecollection.
notes.explanation: RBAC rules are written against these verbs, not against raw HTTP methods.
notes.example: Like translating "knock", "peek", or "open" into the single word a rulebook actually checks.

notes.front: Why are get, list and watch treated as equivalent in terms of data exposure?
notes.back: All three can return the full details of a resource; list on Secrets reveals the data of every matched Secret.
notes.explanation: Granting only list access to Secrets is not a safe half-measure: it still discloses their contents.
notes.example: Like assuming a "browse the shelf" permission is safer than "read one book", when browsing shows every page anyway.

notes.front: What is the system:masters group?
notes.back: A built-in group that grants unrestricted access, bypassing RBAC and Webhook authorizers entirely.
notes.explanation: Because it bypasses those authorizers, removing a RoleBinding can never take this access away from a member.
notes.example: Like a master key that opens every lock in the building, issued outside the normal key-tracking system.

notes.front: What are the default user-facing ClusterRoles?
notes.back: cluster-admin, admin, edit and view: not system:-prefixed, and meant to be bound to real users or groups.
notes.explanation: Custom resources can be added to admin, edit or view by aggregation labels, without editing the built-in ClusterRole.
notes.example: Like a standard set of job titles (owner, editor, viewer) any organisation can hand out.

notes.front: What does the system: prefix on a ClusterRole or ClusterRoleBinding mean?
notes.back: It marks a resource directly managed by the control plane; modifying it can leave the cluster non-functional.
notes.explanation: The API server auto-reconciles these on every start-up, restoring any permissions that go missing.
notes.example: Like factory-fitted wiring in a building: technically editable, but not something you touch casually.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Default roles and role bindings"

notes.front: What does the escalate verb let a user do?
notes.back: Create or update Roles and ClusterRoles with permissions the user does not themselves hold.
notes.explanation: It is the one deliberate exception to RBAC's rule that you can't grant permissions you don't already have.
notes.example: Like a manager who can hand out job titles carrying more authority than their own.

notes.front: What does the bind verb let a user do?
notes.back: Create bindings to Roles or ClusterRoles that carry permissions the user does not already have.
notes.explanation: Like escalate, it bypasses Kubernetes' built-in protection against handing out more access than you hold.
notes.example: Like being allowed to assign any job title to a new hire, even one you don't hold yourself.

notes.front: What does the impersonate verb control?
notes.back: Whether a user can act as, and gain the rights of, another user, group or service account.
notes.explanation: Care is needed granting it, since it can be combined with an impersonated account to reach excessive permissions.
notes.example: Like a pass that lets its holder wear anyone else's badge for the day.

notes.front: What is RBAC privilege escalation prevention?
notes.back: You can only create or update a Role or ClusterRole with permissions you already hold at the same scope, unless you have escalate or bind.
notes.explanation: It is enforced at the API level, so it applies even when the RBAC authorizer is not in use.
notes.example: Like being unable to write a permission slip granting access you don't hold yourself.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Privilege escalation prevention and bootstrapping"

notes.front: Why should wildcard permissions be avoided in RBAC rules?
notes.back: A rule using * grants access to every current resource type, and to every resource type created in the future.
notes.explanation: Because Kubernetes is extensible, a wildcard rule written today can silently cover new CRDs installed tomorrow.
notes.example: Like a permission slip that says "anything, ever" instead of naming what's actually needed.

notes.front: How does permission to create Pods lead to privilege escalation?
notes.back: Anyone who can create Pods in a namespace can mount its Secrets, ConfigMaps and volumes, and run as any ServiceAccount there.
notes.explanation: This is why workload-creation rights should be treated as far more powerful than they look at first glance.
notes.example: Like giving someone a master key to a floor because they only asked to open one office door.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Authorization", "Privilege escalation via workload creation or edits"

notes.front: What does the nodes/proxy permission give access to?
notes.back: The kubelet API, letting the holder run commands in any Pod on the node, bypassing audit logging and admission control.
notes.explanation: Even just get on nodes/proxy is enough, so it is not a read-only permission despite the verb name.
notes.example: Like a permission called "view only" that secretly also lets you flip switches.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "RBAC Good Practices", "Access to proxy subresource of Nodes"

notes.front: What are other RBAC privilege escalation risks besides Pod creation and nodes/proxy?
notes.back: PersistentVolume creation (hostPath), approving CertificateSigningRequests, creating service account tokens, and controlling admission webhooks.
notes.explanation: Each turns a narrow-looking permission into a path to far broader access, so all deserve the same caution as Pod creation.
notes.example: Like several different side doors into the same building, each easy to overlook.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "RBAC Good Practices", "Kubernetes RBAC: privilege escalation risks"

notes.front: Why is periodic access review important for RBAC?
notes.back: To catch redundant entries and possible privilege escalations that have built up over time.
notes.explanation: If an attacker recreates a deleted user's account under the same name, they can inherit that user's old bindings automatically.
notes.example: Like periodically auditing who still holds a key to a building, not just who was ever issued one.

notes.front: What is a SubjectAccessReview?
notes.back: An API object asking whether a given user may perform a given action.
notes.explanation: kubectl auth can-i uses the related SelfSubjectAccessReview to answer the same question for the current user.
notes.example: Like submitting a formal request asking "would this badge open this door?" without actually trying it.

notes.front: What happens to an API request if every configured authorizer returns "no opinion"?
notes.back: It is denied. Access is denied by default.
notes.explanation: An authorizer chain needs at least one module to actively allow a request; silence never grants access.

notes.front: What HTTP status does a denied API request return?
notes.back: 403 Forbidden.
notes.explanation: This is distinct from the 401 Unauthorized a failed authentication returns.

notes.front: What does --authorization-mode=AlwaysAllow,RBAC effectively behave as?
notes.back: The same as AlwaysAllow alone, since RBAC has no deny rules and can never override an earlier allow-everything mode.
notes.explanation: AlwaysAllow grants every request that reaches it, so RBAC never gets a chance to refuse anything.

notes.front: In authorization, what resources can the impersonate verb apply to?
notes.back: users, groups and serviceaccounts in the core API group, and userextras in authentication.k8s.io.
notes.explanation: Knowing the exact resource names matters for writing an RBAC rule that grants only the impersonation you intend.

notes.front: Does membership in system:masters bypass a Webhook authorizer, not just RBAC?
notes.back: Yes. Requests from system:masters members are never even sent to the webhook.
notes.explanation: This makes system:masters strictly stronger than any ClusterRole binding, no matter how permissive.

notes.front: How should you grant someone cluster administrator rights, rather than adding them to system:masters?
notes.back: Create a ClusterRoleBinding to the built-in cluster-admin ClusterRole.
notes.explanation: Unlike system:masters, a ClusterRoleBinding can be reviewed, audited and removed through the normal RBAC objects.

notes.front: How can you add custom-resource permissions to the default admin, edit or view ClusterRoles without editing them directly?
notes.back: Label a new ClusterRole with rbac.authorization.k8s.io/aggregate-to-admin, -edit or -view: "true".
notes.explanation: Aggregation keeps the built-in roles under control-plane management while still letting administrators extend them.

notes.front: Without escalate or bind, at what scope must you already hold a permission to grant it in a new Role or ClusterRole?
notes.back: The same scope as the object being modified: cluster-wide for a ClusterRole, or within the same namespace (or cluster-wide) for a Role.
notes.explanation: This scoping rule is what forces the exception via escalate or bind to be explicit and deliberate.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Restrictions on role creation or update"

notes.front: What general good practice reduces the scope of RBAC rights whenever possible?
notes.back: Assign permissions at the namespace level with RoleBindings, rather than cluster-wide with ClusterRoleBindings.
notes.explanation: A RoleBinding limits the blast radius of a mistaken or compromised grant to one namespace.

notes.front: Why is unrestricted permission to create PersistentVolume objects a privilege-escalation risk?
notes.back: It includes the ability to create hostPath volumes, giving a Pod access to the node's host filesystem.
notes.explanation: Only trusted cluster operators, or the control plane's own provisioning process, should be able to create PersistentVolumes.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "RBAC Good Practices", "Persistent volume creation"

notes.front: How can create rights on CertificateSigningRequests lead to privilege escalation?
notes.back: Combined with approval rights, they let a user mint client certificates with arbitrary names, including names of system components.
notes.explanation: Kubernetes trusts a certificate's identity claims once it is signed and approved, whatever name was requested.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "RBAC Good Practices", "CSRs and certificate issuing"

notes.front: How can rights to create objects lead to a denial-of-service condition?
notes.back: Users can create enough or large enough objects to overload etcd, especially in multi-tenant clusters.
notes.explanation: Resource quotas on object counts are one mitigation for semi-trusted or untrusted users.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "RBAC Good Practices", "Kubernetes RBAC: denial of service risks"

notes.front: What does kubectl auth can-i use to determine if a user can perform an action?
notes.back: The SelfSubjectAccessReview API, so it works regardless of which authorization mode is configured.
notes.explanation: Combined with --as, it can also answer the question for an impersonated user.

notes.front: A team asks for "list" access to Secrets, reasoning that only "get" reveals contents. Should this request be granted as harmless?
notes.back: No. list on Secrets returns the full data of every matched Secret, so it is just as sensitive as get.
notes.explanation: kubectl get secrets -A -o yaml is exactly this kind of list request, and it prints every Secret's contents.

notes.front: A monitoring tool is granted only "get" on nodes/proxy for read-only metrics. Is this actually read-only?
notes.back: No. get on nodes/proxy can retrieve container logs and execute or attach to Pod processes over the kubelet API.
notes.explanation: The verb name suggests a safe read, but the underlying kubelet API it reaches is far more powerful.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "RBAC Good Practices", "Access to proxy subresource of Nodes"

notes.front: A contractor is given rights to create Pods in the billing namespace, but no other permissions there. What can they now effectively reach?
notes.back: Every Secret, ConfigMap and mountable volume in that namespace, and the API access of any ServiceAccount in it.
notes.explanation: This is why creating Pods should be treated as namespace-wide access, not a narrow workload permission.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Authorization", "Privilege escalation via workload creation or edits"

notes.front: A user with no Secret-reading rights is given the escalate verb on clusterroles. Can they now create a ClusterRole that reads all Secrets?
notes.back: Yes. escalate is the specific exception that lets them grant permissions they don't already hold.
notes.explanation: This is exactly why escalate and bind should be handed out as carefully as cluster-admin itself.

notes.front: A Role grants get,list,watch on resources: ["*"] in a namespace. Six months later a new CRD is installed there. What happens to that Role's reach?
notes.back: It automatically covers the new custom resource too, without anyone editing the Role.
notes.explanation: This silent expansion is exactly why wildcard rules are discouraged in favour of naming resource types explicitly.

notes.front: A team wants a quick way to skip authorization while load-testing a local, non-networked test cluster. Is AlwaysAllow acceptable here?
notes.back: Only for testing on a cluster with no untrusted clients; it must never be used where the API server is reachable from the internet.
notes.explanation: The docs single out public reachability as the specific line AlwaysAllow must never cross.

notes.front: An employee named 'jsmith' leaves, and a year later a new hire is also given the username 'jsmith' without a review of old bindings. What risk does this create?
notes.back: The new account can automatically inherit any RoleBindings still pointing at the old, deleted user's name.
notes.explanation: This is exactly the scenario periodic access review is meant to catch before it becomes a real escalation.

notes.front: A support engineer is given impersonate rights on all ServiceAccounts, to debug their permissions. What extra care does this need?
notes.back: Confirming that impersonating any one of those ServiceAccounts cannot itself grant excessive permissions.
notes.explanation: The impersonate verb inherits whatever the impersonated identity can do, so the risk scales with the most powerful account in scope.

notes.front: A cluster wants kubelets to only manage the Pods scheduled to their own node, using an identity-based rule rather than a hand-written RBAC policy. Which mode fits?
notes.back: Node authorization, the special-purpose mode built for exactly this kubelet-to-node relationship.
notes.explanation: It reads the same Pod-to-node bindings the scheduler creates, rather than requiring a custom policy per node.

notes.front: What is the difference between the escalate and bind verbs?
notes.back: escalate lets you create or update a Role or ClusterRole with rights you don't hold; bind lets you attach an existing one to a subject.
notes.explanation: Both bypass the usual "you can only grant what you have" rule, but at different steps: writing the role versus binding it.
notes.contrast: escalate is about authoring extra rights; bind is about handing out rights that already exist.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "RBAC Good Practices", "Escalate verb" and "Bind verb"

notes.front: What is the difference between system:masters and cluster-admin?
notes.back: system:masters is a group that bypasses RBAC and webhook checks entirely; cluster-admin is an ordinary ClusterRole bound to that group by default.
notes.explanation: Removing the default ClusterRoleBinding doesn't help, because system:masters members skip authorization checks regardless of any binding.
notes.contrast: cluster-admin can be reviewed and unbound like any role; system:masters membership cannot be revoked that way.

notes.front: Is there a meaningful data-exposure difference between get, list and watch on Secrets?
notes.back: No. All three can return the full data of a Secret; they differ only in whether you're fetching one, many, or a live stream.
notes.explanation: Treating list as "lighter" than get is a common but incorrect assumption when scoping RBAC rules.
notes.contrast: get names one object; list and watch return or stream many, but every one exposes full contents.

notes.front: What request attributes does Kubernetes authorization actually look at?
notes.back: User, group, extra, whether it is a resource request, request path, verb (API or HTTP), resource, subresource, namespace and API group.
notes.explanation: Because only these attributes are considered, authorization policy can never depend on, say, the request body's contents.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Authorization", "Request attributes used in authorization"

notes.front: What verb does a GET request to /healthz use for authorization, given it isn't a resource endpoint?
notes.back: get: non-resource requests use the lower-cased HTTP method itself as the verb.
notes.explanation: This differs from resource requests, where GET maps to get, list or watch depending on what's being fetched.

notes.front: How does Kubernetes map HTTP methods to resource request verbs?
notes.back: POST is create; GET/HEAD is get, list or watch; PUT is update; PATCH is patch; DELETE is delete or deletecollection.
notes.explanation: This mapping is what lets RBAC rules be written in terms of Kubernetes verbs rather than raw HTTP methods.

notes.front: Besides the standard CRUD verbs, what special-purpose verbs does Kubernetes check for authorization?
notes.back: impersonate (on users, groups, serviceaccounts), approve (on CertificateSigningRequests), and escalate and bind (on roles and clusterroles).
notes.explanation: Each of these checks a narrower, more powerful action than the resource's ordinary verbs.

notes.front: Can --authorization-config and --authorization-mode be set on the API server at the same time?
notes.back: No. Setting both is not allowed; the API server reports an error and exits immediately at start-up.
notes.explanation: You must pick one configuration approach: the file-based authorizer chain, or the older flag-based one.

notes.front: When several authorization modes are listed on the command line, such as --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC,Webhook, what determines priority?
notes.back: The order they're listed in: an earlier module has higher priority to allow or deny the request.
notes.explanation: This ordering is why placing AlwaysAllow first, even alongside RBAC, effectively disables RBAC's checks.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Authorization", "Command line authorization mode configuration"

notes.front: How often does the API server reload the authorization configuration file if no change is observed?
notes.back: Every 60 seconds, in addition to reloading immediately whenever the file does change.
notes.explanation: This gives near-live updates without needing to restart the API server for most authorizer changes.

notes.front: What must stay unchanged when the authorization configuration file is reloaded?
notes.back: Every non-webhook authorizer type: a reload must not add or remove Node or RBAC authorizers, though they can be reordered.
notes.explanation: This keeps a live reload from silently turning a core authorizer on or off.

notes.front: How does an RBAC rule refer to a subresource, such as a Pod's logs?
notes.back: With a slash, as in resources: ["pods", "pods/log"]; access to pods does not itself grant access to pods/log.
notes.explanation: Subresources are authorized separately, so each one that's needed must be listed explicitly.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Referring to resources"

notes.front: What does the resourceNames field on an RBAC rule let you do?
notes.back: Restrict get, update, patch or delete to specific named instances of a resource, rather than every object of that type.
notes.explanation: It narrows an otherwise type-wide grant down to one or a few named objects.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Referring to resources"

notes.front: Can resourceNames restrict a top-level create or a deletecollection request?
notes.back: No. Top-level create can't be named yet at authorization time, and deletecollection can never be restricted by name.
notes.explanation: The create exception does not apply to subresources: resourceNames can still restrict something like pods/exec.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Referring to resources"

notes.front: If list or watch is restricted by resourceName, what must the client's request include to be authorized?
notes.back: A metadata.name field selector matching that resourceName, such as --field-selector=metadata.name=my-configmap.
notes.explanation: Without that field selector, the request doesn't match the narrowed rule and is denied.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Referring to resources"

notes.front: Does cluster-admin always give cluster-wide control, no matter how it's bound?
notes.back: No. Bound with a ClusterRoleBinding it controls the whole cluster; bound with a RoleBinding it controls only that one namespace, including the namespace object itself.
notes.explanation: The same ClusterRole can carry very different real-world scope depending on which kind of binding uses it.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Default roles and role bindings"

notes.front: What can the default admin ClusterRole not do, even inside its own namespace?
notes.back: Write to resource quota, write to the namespace object itself, or write to EndpointSlices, in clusters created with v1.22 or later.
notes.explanation: It still allows creating Roles and RoleBindings in the namespace, which is more than edit is allowed to do.

notes.front: Why does the default edit ClusterRole carry a privilege-escalation risk?
notes.back: It allows accessing Secrets and running Pods as any ServiceAccount in the namespace, gaining that ServiceAccount's API access.
notes.explanation: This is the same privilege-escalation-via-workload-creation risk, now tied specifically to a commonly granted default role.

notes.front: Why does the default view ClusterRole deliberately exclude Secrets?
notes.back: Reading Secret contents would expose ServiceAccount credentials in the namespace, letting the viewer act as any ServiceAccount there.
notes.explanation: This is a rare case where even a strictly read-only default role withholds one resource type entirely, for exactly this escalation reason.

notes.front: A Role grants get and list on pods only. Can its subject run kubectl logs on those Pods?
notes.back: No. Reading logs needs the pods/log subresource listed separately; access to pods alone doesn't cover it.
notes.explanation: Subresources are authorized independently of their parent resource, however closely related they seem.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Referring to resources"

notes.front: A Role should let a subject update only the ConfigMap named my-configmap, not every ConfigMap in the namespace. Which field makes this possible?
notes.back: resourceNames: ["my-configmap"], combined with resources: ["configmaps"] and the needed verbs.
notes.explanation: This narrows a type-wide rule to one specific object, without needing a separate namespace just for that ConfigMap.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Referring to resources"

notes.front: An administrator tries to write a Role rule that allows create only for a ConfigMap named my-configmap, using resourceNames. Will this work as intended?
notes.back: No. Top-level create can't be restricted by resourceNames, since the new object's name isn't known at authorization time.
notes.explanation: This limitation applies only to top-level create, not to subresource actions like pods/exec.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Referring to resources"

notes.front: A user is authorized to list configmaps only when resourceName my-configmap matches. What must their kubectl command include to succeed?
notes.back: A metadata.name field selector for that name, e.g. kubectl get configmaps --field-selector=metadata.name=my-configmap.
notes.explanation: Without that selector, the request doesn't match the narrowed rule and is denied, even though list is otherwise permitted.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Referring to resources"

notes.front: A namespace lead needs to manage Roles and RoleBindings within their own namespace, on top of ordinary read/write access. Which default ClusterRole, bound with a RoleBinding, fits?
notes.back: admin, since edit is explicitly not allowed to view or modify roles or role bindings.
notes.explanation: admin still can't touch resource quota or the namespace object itself, which stays reserved for cluster administrators.

notes.front: Someone bound to the default view ClusterRole runs kubectl get secrets in that namespace. Does it succeed?
notes.back: No. view deliberately excludes Secrets, to stop a read-only viewer from reaching ServiceAccount credentials and escalating.
notes.explanation: It's a useful reminder that "read-only" defaults still withhold specific resources for security reasons.

notes.front: A contractor is granted the default edit ClusterRole in one namespace, meant only for deploying application code. What unintended access does this actually give them?
notes.back: Access to that namespace's Secrets, and the ability to run Pods as any of its ServiceAccounts.
notes.explanation: This is why edit, despite sounding narrow, should be treated as carrying real privilege-escalation risk.

notes.front: A cluster is started with --authorization-mode=Webhook,RBAC. If the webhook returns "deny" for a request that RBAC would have allowed, what is the final verdict?
notes.back: Denied. The first module to give a clear allow or deny wins; RBAC is never even consulted.
notes.explanation: This is exactly why the order authorizers are listed in matters as much as which ones are enabled.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Authorization", "Command line authorization mode configuration"

notes.front: A user can update the certificatesigningrequests/approval subresource but lacks the approve verb for the signer. Can they approve a pending CertificateSigningRequest?
notes.back: No. Approving requires both update rights on the approval subresource and the approve verb for the relevant signer.
notes.explanation: This narrow verb is what keeps approval from being an accidental side effect of broader CertificateSigningRequest management rights.

notes.front: A team wants permission changes to take effect immediately through the API, without editing a file on every control-plane node and restarting it. Should they use ABAC or RBAC?
notes.back: RBAC. ABAC's policies live in a file the API server reads only at start-up, so changes need a restart.
notes.explanation: The apiserver will need to be restarted to pick up new ABAC policy lines, unlike RBAC rules made through the API.

notes.front: Can a normal user rely on Node authorization to gain access to the Pods they personally created?
notes.back: No. Node authorization is a special-purpose mode that grants access only to kubelets, based on the Pods scheduled to their node.
notes.explanation: A human user's access is decided by RBAC, ABAC or Webhook, never by the Node mode.

notes.front: A team is building a custom UI that needs to check, for arbitrary users, whether they can perform an action, without duplicating RBAC logic in the UI itself. What API should it call?
notes.back: SubjectAccessReview, which asks the API server directly whether a given user may perform a given action.
notes.explanation: This keeps the authorization decision in one place, the API server, instead of re-implementing RBAC rules elsewhere.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Controlling Access to the Kubernetes API", "Authorization"

notes.front: What is the difference between the default edit and view ClusterRoles?
notes.back: edit allows read/write on most objects, including Secrets and running Pods as any ServiceAccount; view is read-only and explicitly excludes Secrets.
notes.explanation: view's exclusion of Secrets is deliberate, to avoid the same escalation risk that makes edit powerful.
notes.contrast: edit can act as the namespace's ServiceAccounts; view can only read, and cannot read Secrets.

notes.front: A Role grants verbs: ["*"] on configmaps because the author only wanted get and list. Does this also grant delete?
notes.back: Yes. The verb wildcard grants every current and future verb on that resource, including delete, patch and update.
notes.explanation: This is the same caution the docs give for wildcards in resources: it applies equally to the verbs field.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Referring to resources"

notes.front: A user already holds every permission listed in a new ClusterRole they want to create, but they don't have the escalate verb. Can they still create it?
notes.back: Yes. escalate is only needed when granting permissions you don't already hold; holding them yourself is enough.
notes.explanation: This is the ordinary path the restriction allows: escalate is the exception, not a requirement for every role change.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "Using RBAC Authorization", "Restrictions on role creation or update"

notes.front: An administrator removes a user's ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin, but forgets the user is also in the system:masters group. Can RBAC now restrict them?
notes.back: No. system:masters bypasses all RBAC rights checks, and this cannot be revoked by removing RoleBindings or ClusterRoleBindings.
notes.explanation: The only fix is removing the user from system:masters itself, not adjusting any RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "RBAC Good Practices: Least privilege"

notes.front: A team is granted broad create rights on PersistentVolumes so it can self-provision storage. What escalation risk does this overlook?
notes.back: Creating a hostPath PersistentVolume gives a Pod access to the node's filesystem: a privilege-escalation risk, not just a storage convenience.
notes.explanation: This is why PersistentVolume creation is listed alongside Pod creation and certificate approval as an RBAC escalation risk.
notes.source: Kubernetes documentation, "RBAC Good Practices", "Persistent volume creation"

notes.front: A cluster already runs with --authorization-mode=Node,RBAC. An administrator adds --authorization-config to also configure a Webhook authorizer. Can the API server start with both set?
notes.back: No. Setting --authorization-config and --authorization-mode together makes the API server report an error and exit immediately.
notes.explanation: An administrator must pick one configuration approach: the file-based authorizer chain, or the older flag-based one.
